newsitem.title: JAPAN: INSTANT VIEW - Japan Feb current account surplus.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Japan Feb current account surplus.

text.p: The following is a selection of economists' and analysts' initial reactions to Japan's February current account, which showed a surplus of 865.2 billion yen, slightly higher than economists' average forecast of an 801.1 billion yen surplus.
JESPER KOLL, CHIEF ECONOMIST, J.P. MORGAN
"(It shows) good evidence that Japanese exports benefit from the gain in competitiveness, as well as a pick-up in global demand."

"Head winds (for the Japanese economy) from external account contraction have turned into tail winds and should start to contribute very well to economic growth. Overall, I expect the current account surplus, which now stands at about 1.5 percent of GDP (gross domestic product) to, by the end of this year, stand at about two percent," added Koll.
ANDREW SHIPLEY, ECONOMIST, SCHRODER SECURITIES JAPAN

"There is a clear distortion in the data. One of the main reasons why import growth has been slow in the first quarter of this year was the lack of inventory investment. We're not seeing firms invest in inventories in Japan...as firms attempted to reduce stocks ahead of the consumption tax hike.
"We're now getting clear evidence that the economy is going to continue to expand even with the fiscal tightening this year. This suggests that imports are about to surge.
"This suggests that we will see continued declines in the current account."
JESPER KOLL, CHIEF ECONOMIST, J.P. MORGAN
Koll said he did not expect the figure to trigger a change in the trade policies of either the United States or Japan.

"An expansion of the current account surplus from 1.5 percent to two percent of the GDP over the course of the next 12 months is certainly not at all alarming. In terms of trade implications, we are going to have to see how much further import growth will accelerate in Japan."
